title: Labor's AI guide urges business to 'share benefits'
full_text:
Employers should consult workers before adopting artificial intelligence, codify AI rights in collective agreements and share the benefits through higher pay or shorter hours, the Albanese governments says in draft guidelines about how to adopt the technology.
Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth will on Thursday launch a draft of its first best practice guide on AI in the workplace and said it makes clear workers need to be put at the centre of the adoption process.
The voluntary guide is based on months of departmental roundtable talks with unions, employer groups and experts as well as major companies such as Microsoft, Commonwealth Bank, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores and Ramsay Health Care.
It was released as Labor seeks to balance growing union demands to regulate AI without hindering the productivity potential of the technology, which has become commonplace in Australian workplaces but has a low trust ranking among workers.
Rishworth, who will be the keynote speaker at The Australian Financial Review's AI Forum on Thursday, said the guide meant businesses had a practical road map to "make the most of their AI investment in partnership with their workforce".
"AI adoption is fundamentally about workforce transformation and ultimately, we want AI to enhance Australian workplaces, with businesses and the workforce sharing in the benefits and opportunities it can bring," she said.
Although the guide stresses it does "not create or expand legal obligations", unions are expected to use its recommendations as benchmarks in industrial disputes.
Built on three pillars - planning, enabling and embedding - the guide urges employers to co-operate with workers as early as possible, including "meaningful engagement before a decision is made to introduce AI".
"While businesses remain responsible for making business decisions, they should provide workers with a genuine opportunity to influence decisions on ... AI," it says.
Such approaches can be "embedded through enterprise bargaining", including how workers should be engaged at each stage of AI adoption and how AI-related benefits are shared.
As a model, it pointed to the Finance Sector Union's AI clause with the Australian Retirement Trust, which requires workers to have a voice in AI decisions where the technology will probably automate roles, change capability needs or measure performance.
Rishworth will say in her speech to the AI Forum that the guide accounts for "the dynamic nature of AI adoption, compared to traditional change management exercises".
However, she will warn that many workers "remain anxious about what AI could mean for their jobs, and the community's trust in AI remains low".
"If AI is adopted in ways that increase uncertainty or undermine confidence, it risks slowing the broader adoption and limiting the benefits this technology can deliver."
As a result, the guide urges businesses to provide training to workers for new skills needed for AI during work hours and then consider how to recognise those skills and, "where relevant, reward" them.
Employers should also consider the benefits of AI beyond productivity and plan with workers how to realise those benefits, it said.
"Benefits could include improved wages, shorter working hours, roles shifting towards more meaningful work from which they derive greater job satisfaction, training and skills development in paid work time, greater career advancement opportunities, and more flexible working time."
In the case of Brisbane Catholic College, it points out that 70 per cent of educators reported significant time savings on administration as a result of deep staff consultation. Blackmores' consultation helped reduce three days of manual data entry to ten minutes.
Key trust areas for successful AI adoption include that any AI-informed decisions are explainable and "outcomes are contestable, with human review pathways".
Employers also needed to address the risks of intrusive surveillance, inappropriate performance monitoring and unreasonable work intensification.
Rishworth the draft guideline was open to consultation until January 27.
